answer: Assign a globally unique ID to anything that asks for one. As code: write a function that returns something unique every single time it is invoked (getid() must never return the same value twice).
evidence: Ch1 §1.1: 'Assign a globally unique ID to anything that asks for one. Put as code: write a function that returns something unique every single time it is invoked.'

answer: No. It starts as an ID function that is part of your own application/business logic, called locally on every request (inside every request handler). A central ID service is a later evolution, only if needed.
evidence: Ch1 §1.3: 'Start with an ID function that is part of your own application logic, called locally on every request. A central ID service is an evolution you reach later, only if you need it.' Ch2: 'getid() runs inside every request handler of a service.'

answer: Because time is unique and always moves forward, so returning the current epoch ms (e.g. 1729) is the simplest thing that could work. It is correct only on exactly one machine, and only if the function is never invoked twice within the same millisecond; otherwise both calls get the same value and you'd have to go down to micro- or nanoseconds.
evidence: Ch2 §2.1: 'Time is unique and always moves forward, so the ID function can just return the current epoch millisecond'; 'the function can never be invoked twice within the same millisecond ... you have to go down to micro- or nanoseconds'; 'version 1 is correct on exactly one machine, as long as the code is never called twice within one millisecond.'

answer: Both return 1729, so the IDs collide and are no longer globally unique. Fix: concatenate the machine ID with the epoch ms, concat(machine_id, get_epoch_ms()), giving m1-1729 and m2-1729, unique across both.
evidence: Ch2 §2.2: 'Both can run the function within the same millisecond, and both return the same value, 1729. The IDs collide ... The fix is to concatenate the machine ID with the epoch millisecond: m1-1729 ... m2-1729.'

answer: Whenever you see a collision, add to the ID the thing that led to it (two machines collided, so the machine goes into the ID). Then look for a cheaper alternative to adding it (e.g. a counter instead of thread ID).
evidence: Ch2 §2.2: 'That is the standard move for resolving collisions: whenever you see one, add to the ID the thing that led to it.' Rule box: 'Then look for a cheaper alternative to adding it'.

answer: Because of threads: if the program runs threads on several cores, the function can run twice within the same millisecond on the same machine, and two threads both produce m1-1729.
evidence: Ch2 §2.2: 'Threads break it again. If the program runs threads on several cores, the function can run twice within the same millisecond on the same machine, and two threads both produce m1-1729.'

answer: First, append the thread ID (machine ID + thread ID + epoch ms); second, use an atomically incremented static counter instead of the thread ID.
evidence: Ch2 §2.3: 'That gives two ways to beat thread collisions: append the thread ID, or use an atomically incremented static counter, which works no matter how many threads there are.'

answer: get_id returns concat(machine_id, thread_id, get_epoch_ms()), giving IDs like m1-t1-1729, m1-t2-1729 (and m2-t1-1729, m2-t2-1729). Thread IDs are typically OS-assigned integers; t1, t2 are shorthand.
evidence: Ch2 §2.2 code: 'return concat(machine_id, thread_id, get_epoch_ms()); // m1-t1-1729, m1-t2-1729'; figure: m2-t1-1729, m2-t2-1729.

answer: Always appending the thing that led to the conflict leads to gigantic IDs (every new cause makes the ID longer). A single shared counter avoids that and separates any number of threads.
evidence: Ch2 §2.3: 'always appending the thing that led to the conflict leads to gigantic IDs. A counter avoids that.' 'One shared counter beats any number of threads'.

answer: One globally allocated variable that every thread can reach: one copy per process, shared by all threads (the lecture said it lives on the heap; strictly static storage duration). Its increment must be atomic/thread-safe: counter++ is not atomic by default, so wrap it in a lock/mutex or use the language's native atomic library; then no two threads get the same value.
evidence: Ch2 §2.3: 'one globally allocated variable that every thread can reach ... one copy per process, shared by all threads. Increment it atomically every time'; 'The increment must be thread-safe, and counter++ is not atomic by default. Wrap it in a lock or mutex, or use your language's native atomic library.'

answer: m1-1729-01, m1-1729-02, m1-1729-03, then m1-1730-01 once the millisecond moves on.
evidence: Ch2 §2.3: 'One machine produces m1-1729-01, m1-1729-02, m1-1729-03, then m1-1730-… once the millisecond moves on'; Fig 2c: m1-1730-01.

answer: The atomically incremented counter already increases (differs) on every call, so the time part adds nothing; drop it. The ID becomes machine ID + counter, concat(machine_id, counter++): m1-01, m1-02, m1-03 (m2-01...). Shorter IDs.
evidence: Ch2 §2.3: 'With an atomically increasing counter, the time part is redundant: the counter alone gives 1, 2, 3, … So drop time, and the IDs get shorter: machine ID plus counter, m1-01, m1-02, m1-03.'

answer: Size: the counter can hit the integer limit, about 4 billion (with 2^64 it is so massive you might never hit it). It is also unique only as long as the counter never resets.
evidence: Ch2 §2.3: 'Its one limit is size: the counter can hit the integer limit, which is about 4 billion. With 2^64 it is such a massive number that you might never hit it.' Fig 2c: 'unique as long as the counter never resets.'

answer: It resets to 0 and the machine hands out m1-01, m1-02 again, IDs it already issued, so the logic is no longer unique. Root cause: the counter is stored in volatile memory with no persistence.
evidence: Ch2 §2.4: 'The static counter lived in volatile memory with no persistence, so it resets to 0, and the machine hands out m1-01, m1-02 again ... The root cause is where the counter is stored: volatile memory.'

answer: Back the counter up to a file on disk (labelled fault tolerance on the board). At process start load the counter from disk; on every call increment it, immediately save it to disk, then concat as before: int counter = load(); func get_id() { counter++; save_counter(counter); return concat(machine_id, counter); }. (A plain write lands in page cache; fsync is needed to really survive a crash, and that flush is the expensive part.)
evidence: Ch2 §2.4: 'back the counter up to a file on the machine'; 'when the process starts, load the counter from disk. On every call, increment it, immediately save it to disk ... and then concatenate as before ... labelled fault tolerance'; code shown; fsync note.

answer: 1) Disk pressure: a disk IO per ID, a great many micro disk IOs at thousands of calls/sec. 2) Latency: every ID waits on a disk IO instead of being served from memory.
evidence: Ch2 §2.5: 'the disk takes a lot of pressure from a great many micro disk IOs. That is problem one. Problem two is latency: every ID now waits on a disk IO'.

answer: A really good approach because it tackles the disk IO problem head on (written once per startup, nothing written while IDs are handed out). Costs: the startup increment has to be atomic (it can be made atomic), and the ID gets longer, a third part; only the long ID might become a problem, because long IDs don't index well (chapter 4).
evidence: Ch2 §2.5: 'It has two costs. The increment at startup has to be atomic (it can be made atomic), and the ID gets longer. It is a really good approach, because it tackles the disk IO problem head on. Only the long ID might become a problem'; Ch4 §4.5: 'long IDs don't index well'.

answer: When you read the counter (say 1), add 1000 and store that; serve IDs from memory, and when you reach the stored value read and add 1000 again: a thousand IDs in memory per disk write. I.e., write to disk periodically at a frequency, not every time. Reused for flush-every-N and Amazon's ID service.
evidence: Ch2 §2.5: 'When you read the counter, say it is 1, add 1000 to it and store that. Then serve IDs from memory, and when you reach the stored value, read and add 1000 again: a thousand IDs in memory for each disk write.'

answer:
const N = 1000; // flush frequency
int counter = load() + N; // at startup: past anything issued before
func get_id() { counter++; if (counter % N == 0) save_counter(counter); // one disk write per N IDs
 return concat(machine_id, counter); }
evidence: Ch2 §2.6 code block, as shown.

answer: Because the disk only holds the last flushed value; between flushes the in-memory counter ran ahead and those IDs may already be handed out before a crash. Restarting from load() would reissue them (e.g. disk 6, issued up to 8: restart from 6 regenerates 7 and 8). Adding N jumps past the whole unflushed window to stay clear of anything already issued.
evidence: Ch2 §2.6: 'At startup the counter starts at load() plus the flush frequency, to stay clear of anything already issued'; 'The last value on disk is 6, but 8 was already handed out. Restarting from 6 would generate 7 and 8 again'; 'the restart jumps past the whole window'.

answer: By a factor of 1000 (a massive performance gain). Implement the periodicity as simply as a mod operation: count, take counter mod N, write when it's 0; don't reach for a thread with a timer.
evidence: Ch2 §2.6: 'That cuts disk IO by a factor of 1000'; 'Add a periodicity factor, and keep it as simple as a mod operation: count, take the counter mod N, write. Don't reach for a thread with a timer.'

answer: Disk holds 03 after the first flush, then 06; at the crash the disk still says 6 though 8 was handed out. Safe restart = last flushed + flush frequency + 1 = 6 + 3 + 1 = 10 (load()+N = 9, first ++ gives 10): hands out m1-10, m1-11, m1-12, next flush at 12. Restarting from 6 would duplicate 7 and 8.
evidence: Ch2 §2.6 and Fig 2d: 'after m1-03 the disk holds 03'; 'After six IDs the disk holds 06'; 'start from the safest value: the last flushed value, plus the flush frequency, plus one. In the example that is 6 + 3 = 9, plus 1: 10'; board '06 + 3 + 1 = 09 + 1 = m1-10, Safest !!'.

answer: Some integers are never handed out: 9, and 8 as well if it was still in flight (the lecture counted both 8 and 9 as leaked). Acceptable because correctness of the system matters more than using every single integer: an unused number is fine, a duplicate ID is not.
evidence: Ch2 §2.6: 'Some integers are never handed out: 9, and 8 as well if it was still in flight ... the lecture counted both 8 and 9 as leaked. That is fine. The correctness of the system matters more than using every single integer.' Clip: 'An unused number is fine. A duplicate ID is not.'

answer: 1) Don't do IO every time: add a periodicity factor, as simple as a mod operation (not a timer thread). 2) Whenever a machine recovers, start from the safest value; always think correctness first.
evidence: Ch2 §2.6: 'First, don't do IO every time. Add a periodicity factor, and keep it as simple as a mod operation ... Second, whenever a machine recovers, start from the safest value. Always think of correctness first.'

answer: For conflict resolution (one of the places, not the only one): knowing which came first. Example from the airline check-in: T1 and T2 are ordered by their numbers. A row holds a = 10; T1 sets it to 20, T2 to 30; with newer-write-wins, the larger ID (2) marks the newer write, so accept T2's value, a = 30.
evidence: Ch3 §3.1: 'Think back to the airline check-in ... How did we know transaction T1 came before transaction T2? By their numbers'; 'It holds a = 10; T1 sets it to 20 and T2 sets it to 30 ... the larger number, 2, marks the newer write, so you accept T2's value.'

answer: No. 1 2 3 4 5 6 is what the lecture calls strictly monotonically increasing; 1 2 5 7 8 9 32 33 34 is (just) monotonically increasing: each new ID is greater than all before it, gaps allowed. (In standard terms, strictly increasing with gaps; gap-free is called sequential.)
evidence: Ch3 §3.2: 'Monotonically increasing doesn't mean purely sequential. The lecture calls 1 2 3 4 5 6 strictly monotonically increasing, and 1 2 5 7 8 9 32 33 34 (just) monotonically increasing: each new ID is guaranteed to be greater than all the IDs generated before it.'

answer: Time always moves forward and now sits in the most significant digits/bits, so IDs get a natural order (1729 0001, 1729 0002, 1730 0001); the left half decides order, the right half (machine ID or a counter) only breaks ties. Pretty decent, not strict. Board: 'all ID generation algorithms have time on LHS', under the word sortability.
evidence: Ch3 §3.3: 'concatenate time first, then the machine ID ... it sits in the most significant digits, so the IDs get a natural order'; 'The class board put it as "all ID generation algorithms have time on LHS", under the word sortability.'

answer: Within one millisecond the order can flip: if the first request goes to machine 2 and the next to machine 1, you get 17290002 then 17290001. Only once the millisecond passes are IDs almost monotonic across the system.
evidence: Ch3 §3.3: 'Within one millisecond the order can still flip. If the first request goes to machine 2 and the next one to machine 1, you get 17290002 first and then 17290001.'

answer: It costs almost nothing: still stateless, a request can go to any machine, no central state to maintain, throughput stays excellent; you accept a little incorrectness. With an integer machine ID it's just bits in one number.
evidence: Ch3 §3.3: 'The design is still stateless, so a request can go to any machine; there is no central state to maintain, and throughput stays excellent. In exchange you accept a little incorrectness.'

answer: SRE/DevOps teams run a process that keeps syncing machines' clocks with NTP servers, periodically (more often than you'd think). In practice a daemon (chronyd, ntpd, systemd-timesyncd) runs all the time and disciplines the clock by running it slightly faster/slower; ntpd slews offsets under 128 ms and steps larger ones; slewing limited to 0.5 ms/s.
evidence: Ch3 §3.4: 'SRE and DevOps teams run a process that keeps syncing the machines' clocks with NTP servers'; aside: 'the sync is a daemon (chronyd, ntpd, systemd-timesyncd) ... ntpd slews the clock when the offset is under 128 ms and steps it when the offset is larger'.

answer: A machine's clock is a hardware clock: a quartz crystal vibrating at a frequency, counted to tell time. Physical effects change the vibration: the lecture reasoned heat (e.g. a high-intensity game) makes it vibrate faster so the clock runs fast, extreme cold makes it run slow. More precisely, quartz frequency varies with temperature parabolically (about ±20 ppm, 0.04 ppm/°C² around 25 °C), losing accuracy at both hot and cold.
evidence: Ch3 §3.4: 'a machine's clock is a hardware clock. A quartz crystal vibrates at a particular frequency ...'; 'heat the CPU ... the clock runs fast; ... extremely cold ... the clock runs slow'; More precisely note on ±20 ppm and parabola.

answer: IDs are time then machine number: 232, 244, 237, 239. Not monotonically increasing: m4's clock is a millisecond ahead, so 244 is followed by the smaller 237; arrival order and ID order no longer match, and where order is needed, clock skew affects correctness.
evidence: Ch3 §3.5: 'The IDs come out 232, 244, 237, 239. They are not monotonically increasing.' Check yourself: 'The pair 244 then 237 breaks it: machine 4's clock is a millisecond ahead'.

answer: Google's Jeff Dean and Sanjay Ghemawat once chased a bug that turned out to be a bit flipped by a natural phenomenon (the lecture said an explosion or solar storm). evidence: Ch3 §3.4 aside 'You can't run away from nature'.

answer: Ensuring strict monotonicity across a distributed system where the ID logic runs on many machines is almost impossible; not a theoretical proof (none found), but in practice too many things can break it. Clock skew must be taken care of wherever monotonicity is needed.
evidence: Ch3 §3.5: 'Ensuring strict monotonicity across a distributed system, where the ID logic runs on many machines, is almost impossible. That is not a theoretical proof, and none was found, but in practice too many things can break it.'

answer: One machine hands out every ID: whoever wants an ID makes a network call to the central ID server, which runs the same get_id() with one clock, generates an ID and sends it back (clients 1 and 2 call it). Throughput set aside. Motivation on the board: instead of ID generation in application logic, a central ID service should solve the clock-skew problem. Speech bubble: 'my clock never goes back'.
evidence: Ch3 §3.6 and Fig 3e: 'a central ID generation service: one machine, and whoever wants an ID makes a network call to it; the ID server generates one and sends it back'; 'same get_id(), one clock'.

answer: One machine has one clock, so no skew between generators. When NTP finds the clock ahead (24 when it should be 23), the clock doesn't jump back: it slows its counting until real time catches up, then carries on from 24; the clock never goes back. Caveat: true for small offsets (slewed); larger offsets are stepped and the wall clock can jump backwards, so generators must detect it and wait/refuse (as Snowflake does), use a monotonic clock, or never go below the last value.
evidence: Ch3 §3.6: 'When NTP sync finds the clock is ahead, reading 24 when it should read 23, the clock doesn't jump back. It slows its counting until real time catches up, and then carries on from 24.' More precisely notes on stepping and Snowflake refusing.

answer: It is a single point of failure: the server or its disk could fail. First fix drawn: add one more ID server behind a load balancer for fault tolerance.
evidence: Ch3 §3.7: 'The one ID server is a single point of failure: the server could fail, or its disk could. So for fault tolerance you add one more machine behind a load balancer'.

answer: Whichever server gets a request must first talk to the other server to see its last generated ID, add some buffer, then generate; they gossip constantly on every ID so each new one is larger than any ever generated. evidence: Ch3 §3.7: 'whichever server gets a request has to talk to the other ID server first, to see the last ID it generated, add some buffer on top ... That turns a simple function into something super complex, and it loses throughput'.

answer: 128 bits = 16 bytes. Companies at scale avoid it because every index entry stores the row ID, so a 16-byte ID bloats every index: ~4× vs a 4-byte INT (1 GB → ~4 GB, rough estimate), ~2× vs 8-byte BIGINT; indexes need to fit in RAM to stay fast. answer: A query first builds an execution plan, doing its work on the (tiny) indexes; if they fit in RAM the whole plan (e.g. a join on indexed columns) runs in memory and only the result rows are read from disk at the last step. If an index spills to disk, every lookup becomes a disk read and no other optimization makes it fast.
evidence: Ch4 §4.3: 'the first thing it does is build a query execution plan, and it does that work on the indexes ... If they fit in RAM, a join ... can be done entirely in memory. Only once it knows the result does it go to the disk'; 'If it can't, no amount of other optimization will make it fast.'

answer: Index sizes (random indexes often spilled to disk). Provision DB RAM equal to or more than the total index size: the bare minimum memory is the sum of all index sizes. More precisely, size the buffer pool to hold hot indexes and data, with RAM larger since the cache gets at most ~80%.
evidence: Ch4 §4.3: 'the first thing he checks is index sizes'; 'the RAM of your database server should be equal to or more than your total index size'; 'the bare minimum memory is the sum of the sizes of all the indexes it holds'.

Either works; prefer ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE.
